title: Transaction Cost & Capacity Autopsy: The Backtest That Dies on Implementation
content: A strategy can be statistically genuine — real out-of-sample alpha, clean universe, no look-ahead — and still be economically dead once implementation costs are applied: bid-ask spread, market impact (both temporary price concession during execution and permanent footprint left in the orderbook), financing carry on leveraged positions, and short-borrow fees that can exceed 10-20% annualised for hard-to-borrow micro-cap names. The Almgren-Chriss framework formalises the core trade-off: market impact scales super-linearly with trade size relative to average daily volume (ADV), so a strategy that earns 30 bps per trade at $10M AUM may earn 0 bps net at $200M once impact consumes the alpha — a phenomenon called capacity decay, where realised performance is inversely proportional to assets deployed. The diagnostic fingerprint is distinctive: gross alpha is concentrated in the least-liquid names (smallest ADV, widest spread, highest borrow cost), backtest returns are front-loaded before costs hit, the Sharpe collapses when a realistic half-spread or square-root impact model is applied, and live performance degrades monotonically as AUM grows or as crowding raises market impact and borrow rates simultaneously. High-turnover mean-reversion and small-cap factor strategies are the canonical victims: the very inefficiency they exploit — slow price discovery in thin markets — is also the reason execution costs absorb most or all of the alpha, making capacity, not signal quality, the binding constraint on deployability.
lesson: Gross alpha is not net alpha: a strategy is not validated until it survives a realistic cost model — half-spread on entry and exit, square-root market impact scaled to ADV, financing cost on gross exposure, and borrow-fee drag on the short book — applied at every candidate AUM level; if performance degrades monotonically with size, the strategy has a capacity ceiling, not an edge.
